paras: The Bangor crap-game raid was a raid by Sheriff A. H. Morris of Blount County and a posse on a gathering of Black dice players at Bangor, Alabama, early on a Sunday morning in August 1890, in which a Black man named Jim Thomas was killed. Several other men were slightly wounded and the sheriff received a flesh wound, and the story circulated as a brief wire item in papers in Tennessee, Kentucky, West Virginia and Ohio.

According to a dispatch dated Birmingham, August 12, the raid took place "Early Sunday morning" at Bangor, a place forty miles north of Birmingham, which by the calendar was August 10. Sheriff Morris and his posse raided what the dispatch called "a den of negro crap-shooters," and "a desperate fight ensued." In the fight Jim Thomas was killed, several others were "slightly wounded," and the sheriff took a flesh wound. The dispatch did not say how many men were in the posse or the game, who was armed, or who began the fighting.
The coverage does not name the wounded men and contains no report of arrests, an inquest or any later proceedings.

The Clarksville Daily Tobacco Leaf-Chronicle printed the dispatch with its Birmingham dateline on August 12 under the heading "Crap-Shooter Killed." The same three sentences, stripped of the dateline, then ran in syndicated columns of national briefs in the Richmond, Kentucky, Climax on August 13, the Hickman Courier and the Buckhannon Busy Bee on August 15, and the Logan Ohio Democrat on August 16. In those columns the item sat between unrelated notices of crimes and accidents, unchanged and without comment.

Every version gave only the raiding party's side, identified the dead man by race and by gambling, and offered nothing from the men at the game. No account of the raid was found in the Black press or in an Alabama paper.

reader.title: Bangor crap-game raid
bases: A county sheriff and his posse raided a gathering of Black gamblers and killed one man in the fight that followed (A1).

Jim Thomas was killed, but by a sheriff and posse acting in an official raid on a gambling game, with a fight reported, not by a group acting outside the law under a pretext of justice or tradition (A1); the posse's size is not given.
Every report is the same brief Birmingham wire dispatch (A1), reprinted word for word in A2-A5; no independent or local account was found.
